summary: This standards-track document defines how Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) markings used on wired IP networks are mapped to the User Priority values of IEEE 802.11 wireless networks. Without an agreed mapping, quality-of-service markings can be lost or misapplied when traffic crosses between wired and Wi-Fi segments. It gives implementers a consistent set of mappings so priority treatment carries over.

plainLanguage.summary: Some mail is marked urgent. This tells Wi-Fi how to read the urgent stickers from the wired network so important traffic still gets to cut in line.

subtitle: How to translate wired IP priority markings into Wi-Fi User Priorities so voice, video and data keep the treatment they were meant to get.

tldr.problem: The common way of turning a 6-bit DSCP into a 3-bit Wi-Fi User Priority (copy the top three bits) puts voice in the video queue, streaming video in best effort and operations traffic in background, and the usual reverse mapping loses detail.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8325 recommends an explicit DSCP-to-UP table built on the RFC 4594 service classes (for example EF to UP 6, AF4x to UP 4, DF to UP 0), plus rules for upstream marking, with a strong lean toward the access point re-marking DSCP itself.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8325 is a Proposed Standard from February 2018. It has been updated by RFC 8622 and RFC 9956, and its mappings may be overridden by administrators.

today: RFC 8325 is a Proposed Standard from February 2018 and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8622 and RFC 9956. Check those RFCs for changes to its recommended mappings.

sections.title: The Wired-to-Wireless QoS Gap
sections.content:
IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) is the preferred way for endpoints to join business and private networks, but it makes end-to-end quality of service (QoS) hard. The medium is half-duplex and shared, and the 802.11 standard is run by a different body than the IP standards. The IEEE built QoS tools, yet little guidance existed on keeping wired IP treatment consistent across Wi-Fi. RFC 8325 supplies that guidance.

The mapping starts from the service classes of RFC 4594, which tells operators which DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) to use for each kind of traffic. The DSCP sits in the first 6 bits of the IPv4 TOS field or IPv6 Traffic Class field. Wi-Fi marks frames with a 3-bit User Priority (UP), valued 0 to 7.

The document applies to any Wi-Fi infrastructure at the link layer, whether APs are autonomous or run by controllers, including backhaul and mesh. It also explains why it does not align with the GSMA-derived RFC 7561: that plan conflicts with the overall Diffserv plan, so the two are treated as different Diffserv domains separated by a boundary where codepoints are translated.
sections.plainLanguage: Wired networks and Wi-Fi use different ways of saying "this is important." Nobody had written down how to translate between them.

sections.title: Why the Default Mappings Fail
sections.content:
Many systems use a default DSCP-to-UP mapping: take the three most significant bits of the DSCP as the UP. Applied to RFC 4594 markings, this gives inconsistent results:

  • Voice (EF) goes to UP 5, so it lands in the Video Access Category (AC_VI) instead of Voice (AC_VO).
  • Multimedia Streaming (AF3x) and Broadcast Video (CS3) go to UP 3 and land in Best Effort (AC_BE), not Video.
  • OAM traffic (CS2) goes to UP 2 and lands in Background (AC_BK), against the intent of RFC 4594.

The reverse, the default UP-to-DSCP mapping, multiplies the UP by 8. Going from three bits to six loses information: only eight classes can be told apart, not the twelve of RFC 4594, and UP 7 (CS7) is effectively reserved. UP 6 becomes CS6, which RFC 4594 reserves for Network Control, while Multimedia Conferencing and Real-Time Interactive both become CS4 and cannot be separated.

The RFC also notes that 802.11 cannot give true Expedited Forwarding or Assured Forwarding service, because contention for the channel has a random element. It only loosely supports the Default PHB (via AC_BE) and the Lower Effort PDB (via AC_BK).
sections.plainLanguage: If you translate by only looking at the first part of a sticker, a rush-delivery sticker can end up in the "video" pile and a routine one in the "background" pile. The old shortcut gets lots of them wrong.

sections.title: How 802.11 QoS Works
sections.content:
Original Wi-Fi used the Distributed Coordination Function (DCF), a collision avoidance scheme (CSMA/CA) based on timers. A station waits for the medium to be idle for a DIFS, then waits an extra random backoff bounded by a contention window (CW). The CW roughly doubles after each collision until it reaches CWmax.

The Hybrid Coordination Function (HCF) added QoS. A QoS Control field carries a 3-bit User Priority, and the standard fixes how pairs of UPs map to four Access Categories: UP 7 and 6 to AC_VO (Voice), UP 5 and 4 to AC_VI (Video), UP 3 and 0 to AC_BE (Best Effort), and UP 2 and 1 to AC_BK (Background).

Categories get different treatment by tuning timers. The arbitration interframe space (AIFS) is 2 slot times for voice and video, 3 for best effort and 7 for background. CWmin and CWmax are 3 and 7 for voice, 7 and 15 for video, and 15 and 1023 for both best effort and background. Voice therefore gets statistically better service than video, then best effort, then background. A UP value on its own changes nothing over the air; only the fixed mapping to an access category does.

IEEE 802.11u also defines a QoS Map element, sent from an AP to a client, that tells the client how DSCP ranges map to the eight UPs, with up to 21 exceptions.
sections.plainLanguage: Wi-Fi is like one room where everyone talks at once. Urgent talkers are allowed to wait a shorter, luckier time before speaking, so they usually get their turn first.

sections.title: The Recommended DSCP-to-UP Mapping
sections.content:
For the downstream (wired to wireless) direction, the RFC maps each RFC 4594 service class to a UP. The wireless AP and endpoints are assumed to support marking DSCP and UP and fully configurable mappings between them.

  • Network Control: CS6 and CS7 are RECOMMENDED to map to UP 7 (AC_VO), but see the security rules below, which prefer UP 0 where the AP is the network edge.
  • Telephony (EF) and VOICE-ADMIT (DSCP 44): UP 6, in AC_VO.
  • Signaling (CS5): UP 5, in AC_VI.
  • Multimedia Conferencing (AF41 to AF43), Real-Time Interactive (CS4), Multimedia Streaming (AF31 to AF33) and Broadcast Video (CS3): UP 4, in AC_VI.
  • Low-Latency Data (AF21 to AF23): UP 3, in AC_BE.
  • OAM (CS2), High-Throughput Data (AF11 to AF13) and Standard (DF): UP 0, in AC_BE.
  • Low-Priority Data (CS1): UP 1, in AC_BK.

High-Throughput Data has no good fit in the four-category model, so UP 0 is chosen. All unused codepoints are RECOMMENDED to map to UP 0. The mappings are not expected to fit every deployment, so administrators MAY override them.
sections.plainLanguage: Here is the new translation chart. Phone calls go to the fastest lane, video to the next, ordinary mail to the middle lane, and "whenever you get to it" mail to the slowest lane.

sections.title: Upstream Mapping and Marking
sections.content:
In the upstream (wireless to wired) direction, three options exist: DSCP-to-UP mapping inside the client operating system, UP-to-DSCP mapping at the AP, or DSCP passthrough at the AP. The RFC prefers a fourth: make the wireless edge a Diffserv boundary and have the AP set or reset DSCP by administrative policy. This is RECOMMENDED over mapping whenever the AP can do it, because the network administrator, not an application or OS developer, enforces the policy.

Client operating systems are RECOMMENDED to use the same Section 4 mapping, but packets requesting CS6 or CS7 SHOULD be mapped to UP 0 and re-marked to DSCP 0, because network control markings SHOULD NOT come from wireless clients. APs MUST NOT map the UPs set by wireless hosts into DSCP in the upstream direction. If host markings are to be honoured, the AP should pass through the Layer 3 DSCP instead, except CS6 and CS7, and it is generally NOT RECOMMENDED to pass through DSCP from unauthenticated or unauthorized devices.

When the QoS Map element is used, the RFC recommends mapping each of the eight UPs to DSCP 0 as a baseline, with up to 21 exceptions that follow the Section 4 table for codepoints in use. That element assumes the AP is the edge of the Diffserv domain.
sections.plainLanguage: For mail going back the other way, the best idea is for the post office to put on its own fresh sticker instead of trusting whatever the sender wrote.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says its recommendations add no new security concerns, and several protect against abuse. A device can mark packets to jump the queue; the RFC's example is a game that marks all traffic EF or UP 6 and interferes with business voice. Recommended measures include a traffic conditioning policy that bleaches (re-marks to DF or UP 0) traffic from unauthorized sources and policing of EF flows.

Wi-Fi is an especially easy denial-of-service target, because clients contend with the AP on equal terms. A client could monopolize the air by sending traffic marked to UP 4 through 7, so the ability to mark or map to those values should be controlled. For example, a flood of CS7 downstream maps by default to UP 7 and AC_VO and could starve every other class.

Therefore any codepoint not authorized for the wireless network SHOULD be mapped to UP 0 at the AP (downstream) and in the client OS (upstream). In the common Wi-Fi-at-the-edge model, where only clients sit below the AP, CS6 and CS7 are among those unused codepoints, so they are RECOMMENDED to map to UP 0. The RFC adds that it does not address every QoS abuse vector and lists authentication, access control, rate limiting and other measures as complements.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone could stamp "super urgent" on their mail, the real urgent mail would never get through. So the rules say to ignore stickers that nobody approved.

sections.title: Scope and Status
sections.content: RFC 8325 contains no IANA actions. Its mappings are RECOMMENDED to replace common default practice but may be overridden. The RFC notes that the Low-Priority Data marking may change in future, because a separate Lower Effort PHB document (a work in progress when RFC 8325 was written) proposes an additional DSCP for that traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The chart is a strong suggestion, not a law. Each network can tweak it for its own needs.
